newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Capitalism catching on fast in east Europe - report.
newsitem.headline: Capitalism catching on fast in east Europe - report.

text.p: Millions of firms have been created in central and eastern Europe since the collapse of communism but many of them are struggling to survive, according to a survey published by the European Commission on Wednesday.
"Too many enterprises have been set up and some are likely to disappear," the survey said.

Six years after the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989, 3.4 million companies were operating in market economy conditions in 11 central and eastern European countries eager to join the 15-nation European Union, it added.

Most firms were established during the period of economic reform in the 1990s and are very small said the survey by Eurostat, the EU's statistics office, and the statistical offices of the applicant countries.
"A whole new social group of small entrepreneurs has been born," Eurostat said, adding that more than half the firms operated from their founders' homes.

In all countries, with the exception of the three Baltic states and Albania, the proportion of firms created through the privatisation of former state companies or splitting up of cooperatives is negligible.
"The vast majority have been created from scratch with no inherited structures of former state enterprises."

However, it also made clear that many firms suffered severe problems and went under soon after they were set up. For every 100 active firms, 18 were dormant but hoped to start or resume work while another 55 said they were "definitely dead".
Sixty-one percent of active companies admitted serious difficulties in surviving or developing and more than half of them complained about production difficulties.
"Most common were absence of resources, lack of credit facilities and delays and defaults in customer payments," Eurostat said.
"These very small enterprises -- 66 percent of which do not have any salaried employees -- are still fragile due to difficulties in accumulating capital and securing investment."
There were 31 companies per 1,000 inhabitants on average, in contrast to the EU ratio of 43 per 1,000.
"Structure by size and sector of activity is already similar to that in the EU," Eurostat said.
Of the 3,362,121 firms logged in September last year, nearly a third were in Poland, over a fifth in the Czech Republic and over 15 percent in Hungary.
"The density is closely linked to GNP (gross national product) per head," Eurostat said.

Medium and large firms accounted for a similar proportion in the EU and in the 11 central and eastern European countries -- Poland, the Czech Republic, Hungary, Romania, Bulgaria, Slovakia, Slovenia, Lithuania, Albania, Estonia and Latvia.
In comparison with the EU, the applicant countries have a larger proportion of manufacturing companies but fewer firms active in construction, distribution, transport and services.
Almost 10 percent of the 486,000 public and private limited liability companies depended on foreign capital.
"In the total number of enterprises, foreign capital participation was very low but such firms accounted for 10.8 percent of jobs," Eurostat said.
